# Data in BiologyToMath: everything is generated by code

The repository stores **no data files and no pictures**. Every data set, figure and diagram in the
29 notebooks is produced by code that runs inside the notebook. Data come from the simulators in
[`course_toolkit.py`](course_toolkit.py) (copied verbatim into each notebook that uses them), from
small simulation functions written in the notebook itself, or from short classic tables typed into
a cell and labelled as such (Mendel's peas, Bortkiewicz's horse kicks, the genetic code, …).

Why simulate?

- **A known truth.** Every simulator returns the hidden truth it was built from — the genes that
  really respond to infection, the true expression rate of every gene in every cell type, the true
  allele frequency, the true drug effect, the true regression coefficients — so every estimate,
  test and decomposition in the course can be *checked*: did the MLE recover the rate, did the
  t-test find the effect, did Benjamini–Hochberg keep the false discoveries below 5 %?
- **Numbers you can check by hand.** A mathematics course needs examples small enough to compute on
  paper. The classic worked examples are typed in with their exact numbers, and the code reproduces
  each hand calculation.
- **A slim, self-contained repository.** Nothing to download, no licences to track, no broken links;
  every notebook runs offline on a free CPU in about two minutes.
- **Reproducible.** Every simulator has a fixed default seed and every notebook sets `SEED = 0`, so
  every notebook (and every student) sees the same data and the same numbers.

What simulation cannot teach — the messiness of real data (batch effects, missing values, outliers,
unknown truth) — is discussed in the 🌉 *Bridge* boxes and taken up in the sister course
[BiologyToML](../../../ml/tutorial/BiologyToML/README.md). The simulators reproduce the *structure* of
real experiments (sizes, typical effect sizes, noise levels, overlaps); they never claim to reproduce
published numbers, and the notebooks say so.

## Simulators and constants in the course toolkit

Module lists give every notebook whose code calls the simulator or uses the constant (checked against the notebooks).

| Toolkit name | Mimics | What it returns (hidden truth in **bold**) | Modules |
|---|---|---|---|
| `simulate_tissue_expression()` (seed 2680) | a multi-tissue infection experiment: log2 gene expression in spleen, kidney and liver, 4 control and 4 infected samples each (24 samples × 400 genes); the 12 named infection-response genes respond in every tissue, further genes in one or two tissues, so the sets of changed genes overlap like those of a real multi-tissue study; 12 housekeeping genes are stable; about a third of genes differ in baseline between tissues | `X` (samples × genes), `samples` (sample, tissue, condition), `genes`, **`true_lfc`** (true infected − control difference per tissue and gene), **`true_de`** (tissue → set of truly changed genes: 51 in spleen, 44 in kidney, 35 in liver; 12 shared by all), `pathways`, `source` | 00, 01, 03, 06, 07, 08, 10, 12, 13, 19, 21, 25, 26, 27, 28 |
| `INFECTION_PATHWAYS` | three innate-immune programmes of real infection-induced genes: cytokine signalling (IL1B, TNF, IL6, CXCL8), interferon response (IRF1, STAT1, MX1, ISG15), acute phase (SAA1, HAMP, C3, and the antimicrobial enzyme LYZ, grouped here for simplicity) | a dict pathway → genes; these genes are **the shared response set** of `simulate_tissue_expression` | 01 (sets of genes), 07 (signature scores), 08 (pathway scores), 21 (variance ranks), 26 (enrichment), 28 (pathway scores, enrichment); and, inside the simulator, every module that uses the infection experiment |
| `HOUSEKEEPING_GENES` | classic qPCR reference genes (ACTB, GAPDH, EEF1A1, RPL13A, TBP, HPRT1, PPIA, UBC, YWHAZ, SDHA, TUBA1A, B2M) | a list; in the simulator these genes are **stable** (noise SD 0.08, no response) | 00 (a set of genes), 07 (a housekeeping direction), 21 (variance ≈ 0 vs highly variable genes), 26 and 28 (negative-control gene set); and inside every use of the infection experiment |
| `INFLAMMATION_NETWORK_EDGES` | a simplified, illustrative cartoon of innate-immune signalling: NF-κB induces cytokines, TNF and IL-1β activate NF-κB (a feedback loop), IL-6 acts through STAT3 on acute-phase genes, STAT1 induces interferon-stimulated genes | 15 directed (regulator → target) edges among 14 genes | 06 (degrees, hubs, cycles, induced subgraphs), 08 (adjacency-matrix powers), 12 (eigenvector centrality), 28 (the discoveries on the network) |
| `simulate_cell_counts()` (seed 680) | single-cell RNA counts of four immune and stromal cell types (160 T cells, 120 B cells, 90 macrophages, 70 fibroblasts) × 40 genes; Poisson counts, or negative-binomial with `overdispersion` φ > 0 | `counts` (cells × genes), **`labels`** (true cell type of each cell), `genes`, **`rates`** (true mean count λ of every gene in every cell type), `source` | 09 (cell-type deconvolution of a pseudo-bulk sample), 11 (signature matrix and rank), 17 (Poisson naïve Bayes), 18 (Poisson counts), 21 (mean–variance relationship, over-dispersion), 23 (Poisson MLE per cell type), 28 (MLE vs MAP rates, a model violation) |
| `CELL_TYPE_MARKERS` | three real marker genes per cell type (T cell: CD3E, CD3D, IL7R; B cell: CD79A, MS4A1, CD19; macrophage: CD68, LYZ, CSF1R; fibroblast: COL1A1, COL1A2, DCN) | a dict cell type → markers; in the simulator markers are **high (λ ≈ 6–15) in their own type, low (≈ 0.1–0.5) elsewhere** | 09, 11, 21, 23; and inside the simulator, every module that uses `simulate_cell_counts` |
| `simulate_genotypes(n, p, inbreeding)` (seed 1866) | genotypes of n diploid individuals at one SNP, coded 0/1/2 copies of an allele, under Hardy–Weinberg proportions or with an inbreeding coefficient F that moves heterozygotes to homozygotes | an array of 0/1/2; the truth is the **allele frequency p** and **F** you pass in | 11 (the genotype-coding trap in a design matrix), 16 (genotype relative frequencies), 18 (genotypes as Binomial(2, p)), 19 (genotype × disease table), 22 (polygenic trait, standard error of an allele frequency), 23 (allele-frequency MLE), 26 (Hardy–Weinberg χ² test), 27 (a miniature GWAS) |
| `simulate_cholesterol_trial(n, effect)` (seed 2026) | a paired drug trial: LDL cholesterol (mg/dL) of 12 patients before and after treatment; patients differ a lot from each other (SD 30 around 160), day-to-day noise is smaller (SD 10) | a table patient, before, after; the truth is the **average drug effect** (default −18 mg/dL) | 22 (confidence interval for the mean change), 25 (paired vs unpaired t-test, power), 28 (design and analyse a cholesterol trial) |
| `simulate_insulin_study(n)` (seed 1921) | a clinical study of 120 adults: fasting insulin (µU/mL) as a linear function of BMI, age and fasting glucose (glucose itself correlated with BMI and age) plus Gaussian noise | a table bmi, age, glucose, insulin | 15 (least squares by the normal equations and by gradient descent), 27 (multiple regression with inference) |
| `INSULIN_TRUE_COEFFICIENTS`, `INSULIN_TRUE_SIGMA` | the hidden truth of the insulin study | **intercept −4.0, BMI 0.55, age 0.04, glucose 0.06; noise SD 2.5** | 15, 27 |
| `simulate_dna(length, transitions, initial)` (seed 0) | DNA sequence: i.i.d. uniform bases, or a first-order Markov chain with a given 4 × 4 transition matrix | a string over {A, C, G, T}; the truth is the **transition matrix** used (and, where a notebook embeds a CpG island, its **position**) | 01 (a random word), 04 (k-mers, dinucleotides), 05 (timing algorithms, k-mer counting), 06 (a sequence for a de Bruijn graph), 12 (stationary base composition), 16 (a stretch of DNA as a sample space), 17 and 19 (are neighbouring bases independent?), 20 (CpG-island detection), 28 (a CpG-island detector) |
| `CPG_ISLAND_TRANSITIONS`, `BACKGROUND_TRANSITIONS` | the classic first-order Markov models of CpG islands ("+") and of background sequence ("−") estimated from human DNA by Durbin *et al.* (1998), Table 3.1, rounded to two decimals; in islands a C is often followed by a G, elsewhere CG is rare because methylated C in CpG mutates to T | two 4 × 4 row-stochastic matrices, rows = current base, columns = next base, order A, C, G, T | 20 (P(ACTTC ∣ island) = 0.000831 vs P(ACTTC ∣ background) = 0.001044; log-odds scan); both matrices also in 04, 12, 19 and 28, the background matrix alone in 13 (Pⁿ by diagonalization) and 17 (probability of a string) |
| `NUCLEOTIDES`, `COMPLEMENT` | the DNA alphabet and Watson–Crick base pairing | ("A", "C", "G", "T"); A↔T, C↔G | `NUCLEOTIDES`: 04, 19, 20, 28; `COMPLEMENT`: 03 |

The other toolkit helpers produce no data; they draw or compute: `implies`, `iff`, `xor`,
`truth_table` (00, 02), `jaccard` (03, 26, 28), `draw_venn` (00, 02, 03, 16, 26, 28),
`circle_layout` (06), `tree_layout` (04, 06), `adjacency_matrix` (06, 08, 12, 28), `draw_graph` (02,
04, 06, 08, 09, 12, 20, 28), `plot_vectors` (07, 10–13, 15), `format_matrix` (08, 09, 11–13),
`gauss_jordan` (09, 11), `reverse_complement` (03, 04), `kmer_counts` (04, 05, 06),
`markov_log_probability` (20, 28).

A curiosity worth knowing before you experiment: with its default seed (1866),
`simulate_genotypes(500, 0.3)` happens to return exactly the Hardy–Weinberg expected counts
245 / 210 / 45, so a χ² test on it gives X² = 0 — a fluke of that seed, not a property of the
simulator. The notebooks that test such a sample pass another seed (Module 23 uses `seed=7`:
231 / 226 / 43) so that you see ordinary sampling noise.

## Classic tables typed into the notebooks

These are short worked-example tables from the classic literature or from standard textbook
examples, typed into the cell that uses them and labelled as typed-in (nothing is downloaded).

| Table | Values | Modules |
|---|---|---|
| Mendel's dihybrid cross (Mendel 1866) | round-yellow 315, wrinkled-yellow 101, round-green 108, wrinkled-green 32 (n = 556), against the 9:3:3:1 hypothesis | 01 and 16 (quoted in the text after the dihybrid-cross examples), 26 (typed in; χ² goodness of fit; Fisher's "too good to be true" critique) |
| Bortkiewicz's horse-kick deaths (Bortkiewicz 1898) | deaths per Prussian army corps per year in 200 corps-years: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 deaths observed 109, 65, 22, 3, 1 times (mean 0.61) | 18 (observed vs Poisson expected counts; exponential waiting times) |
| CpG-island and background transition matrices (Durbin *et al.* 1998) | the two 4 × 4 matrices above (kept in the toolkit) | 20 (also 04, 12, 13, 17, 19, 28) |
| The standard genetic code | 64 codons → 20 amino acids + stop, typed as a Python dict | 01 (a dict is a finite function), 03 (the genetic code as a many-to-one function), 04 (codons and reading frames), 17 and 19 (only the three stop codons TAA, TAG, TGA and the dependence between codon positions) |
| The telephone-line Markov chain (a classic textbook example; cf. DeGroot & Schervish) | 6 states (0–5 lines in use), initial distribution v = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0, 0, 0) and a 6 × 6 transition matrix; P(no line in use three steps after all five are in use) = 0.116; vP² = (0.133, 0.227, 0.202, 0.156, 0.162, 0.120) | 20 |
| The weather Markov chain | sunny/cloudy, P = [[0.7, 0.3], [0.6, 0.4]]; sunny on Wednesday → P(sunny on Saturday and Sunday) = 0.667 × 0.7 ≈ 0.467 | 20 |
| The bronchitis Bayesian network (a textbook toy model) | P(S) = 0.4 (smokes), P(C) = 0.8 (cold); P(T ∣ S, C) = 0.35, P(T ∣ ¬S, C) = 0.25, P(T ∣ S, ¬C) = 0.1, P(T ∣ ¬S, ¬C) = 0.05 (bronchitis); P(O ∣ T) = 0.6, P(O ∣ ¬T) = 0.15 (cough); P(A ∣ T) = 0.5, P(A ∣ ¬T) = 0.1 (asthma) — illustrative | 20 (P(T ∣ S) = 0.30 and further queries) |
| The X → Y → Z network | small conditional probability tables (P(X) = 0.7/0.3, P(Y ∣ X), P(Z ∣ X, Y) and the chain version P(Z ∣ Y)) | 20 |
| The BRCA1/P53/cancer joint table | P(G₁, G₂, C) = 0.24, 0.01, 0.20, 0.05, 0.15, 0.10, 0.05, 0.20 → P(cancer ∣ G₁, G₂) = 0.04, 0.20, 0.40, 0.80 — **illustrative numbers, not clinical estimates** | 19 (a simple classifier with uncertainty) |
| Gene expression and disease risk | a joint table of "gene A high" × disease in 1,000 individuals — illustrative | 19 |
| The flu/cough joint table | P(flu, cough) = 0.3, P(flu, no cough) = 0.2, P(no flu, cough) = 0.15, P(neither) = 0.35 → P(flu ∣ cough) = 2/3 | 17 |
| Flu diagnosis by Bayes' rule | prior 0.05, P(cough ∣ flu) = 0.8, P(cough ∣ no flu) = 0.2 → 0.174 (and 0.8 with prior 0.5) — illustrative | 17 |
| The coin examples | the two-coin box (a fair and a two-headed coin), the die events A = {1,2}, B = {2,4,6}, C = {1,4}, the unfair-coin joint tables, the spam filter (P(S) = 0.7, 0.9, 0.01), the coin drawer (5, 3, 2 coins with heads probability 0.5, 0.6, 0.9), the discrete prior over θ ∈ {0.2, 0.5, 0.7} | 17 (two-coin box, die events, spam filter), 19 (unfair-coin tables), 24 (coin drawer, discrete prior) |

## Illustrative numbers

Some modules use realistic but **illustrative** parameters, labelled as such in the notebook; they
show how the mathematics works and are not estimates for any real patient, drug or population:
screening-test sensitivity, specificity and prevalence (00, 17, 24, 28) and BRCA1 carrier risks
(17); the BRCA1/P53 table (19); one-compartment pharmacokinetics (C₀, elimination rate k, half-life,
AUC) and Michaelis–Menten constants (V_max, K_m) (01, 14, 15, 28); growth rates and carrying
capacities of bacterial cultures (01, 10, 14); the tRNA charging model's production, binding,
unbinding and degradation rates and the SIR model's β and γ (15); Leslie-matrix fecundities and
survival probabilities (12, 13, 28); a small distance matrix of four or five species for a
phylogenetic tree (06); a toy metabolic pathway's stoichiometric matrix (09, 10, 11); the students ×
classes, users × movies and similar toy matrices (08, 13).

## Small simulations written in the notebooks

Several notebooks add their own short simulations, documented where they are defined: the state
transitions of a three-gene Boolean network (02); random sequences for timing algorithms (05);
expression "programmes" plus noise to show rank and singular values (11, 13); co-expressed genes as
a bivariate normal (19); a Leslie-matrix population projection (12, 13); growth curves,
pharmacokinetic curves and Euler's method (14); trajectories of gradient descent, the tRNA model and
an SIR epidemic, and noisy Michaelis–Menten measurements for Gauss–Newton fitting (15); coins, dice,
a site-frequency spectrum and Punnett-square crosses (16); sequences with an embedded CpG island
(20); running means, polygenic traits as sums of many small effects, and 100 repeated confidence
intervals (21, 22); p-values under the null (25, 26).

---

## Rules for contributors

- Do not add data files, pictures, downloads or file reads. The validator
  (`python validate_notebooks.py`) rejects stored data and picture files, files over 400 kB,
  embedded or linked pictures (the Colab badge is the only external image), and code that downloads
  or reads data.
- Generate data with the toolkit or with a documented simulation function in the notebook; return
  the hidden truth and compare the result with it.
- Label simulated data (print the `source` line, put "SIMULATED" in plot titles and in the code-cell
  header), label illustrative numbers as illustrative, and label typed-in tables with their origin.
- Keep typed-in tables to a few lines; they are worked examples, not data sets.
- If a new simulator is useful to several notebooks, add it to `course_toolkit.py`, then rebuild
  every notebook that copies it (the validator reports copies that differ) and update this file.
